items.stem: First presentation of acute non-specific low back pain, no red flags, no leg symptoms. What does every major guideline agree is first-line management?
options: Reassurance, advice to stay active, and early return to normal activity
Bed rest until the pain settles
Early MRI to identify the pain source
Referral for spinal injection
items.explanation: NICE, ACP, and WHO guidelines converge: education, reassurance about the benign course, staying active, and early return to activity. Bed rest delays recovery, early imaging worsens outcomes via incidental findings, and injections have no role in acute non-specific LBP.
items.pearl: The strongest 'treatment' for acute NSLBP is preventing iatrogenic fear.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: Which situation actually justifies lumbar imaging?
options: Progressive neurological deficit or suspected serious pathology
Pain lasting more than 2 weeks
Patient anxiety and a desire to 'see what's wrong'
Pain radiating to the buttock
items.explanation: Image when the result would change management: red flags, progressive neuro deficit, or surgical planning. Disc degeneration appears in ~37% of asymptomatic 20-year-olds and ~96% of asymptomatic 80-year-olds — routine imaging finds 'abnormalities' in nearly everyone and predicts almost nothing.

items.stem: During repeated extension movements, a patient's leg pain retreats from the calf to the buttock while their central back pain briefly increases. What does this 'centralization' mean?
options: A favourable prognostic sign — this movement direction is worth exploiting in treatment
The disc is being further damaged
The patient needs urgent imaging
The leg pain was psychosomatic
items.explanation: Centralization — distal symptoms retreating proximally with repeated movement — predicts good outcome and identifies a directional preference to build treatment around. The transient increase in central pain during centralizing movements is expected, not a warning.
items.pearl: Track WHERE the pain is, not just how much. Location shift beats intensity change as a signal.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: A worried patient with 1 week of acute low back pain asks what to expect. What's the honest, evidence-based answer?
options: Most people improve substantially within 6 weeks, though mild symptoms and recurrences are common
This will probably become chronic
Nothing can be predicted
Full recovery within 3 days is typical
items.explanation: Acute LBP has a strongly favourable natural history: rapid early improvement, most substantial recovery within ~6 weeks. Honest framing includes the caveats — recurrence within a year is common (~33%+) and a minority develop persistent pain, which is why yellow-flag screening matters at the start.

items.stem: Which factor most strongly predicts an acute episode of LBP becoming persistent and disabling?
options: Fear-avoidance beliefs, catastrophizing, and low recovery expectations
The size of disc bulge on MRI
Severity of pain on day one
Body weight
items.explanation: Psychosocial factors (yellow flags) outperform imaging findings and initial pain severity in predicting chronicity. A patient who believes their back is fragile and stops moving is at greater risk than one with a bigger bulge who stays active. Tools like the STarT Back screen exist precisely to catch this early.
items.pearl: The MRI predicts less than the patient's beliefs do.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: You suspect an L5/S1 disc herniation, but the straight leg raise is negative. Best conclusion?
options: Disc herniation is now considerably less likely — SLR is a rule-OUT test
The result changes nothing
Herniation is confirmed at a higher level
Sensitivity 91% means a negative test rules the diagnosis in
items.explanation: High sensitivity (91%) means the SLR catches nearly all disc herniations — so a NEGATIVE result meaningfully lowers probability (SnNout, LR− 0.35). Its terrible specificity (26%) is why a positive SLR proves little on its own.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: Raising the patient's LEFT leg reproduces their RIGHT leg pain (positive crossed SLR). Best conclusion?
options: A strong pointer toward disc herniation — this test rarely false-positives
The pain must be non-organic
This rules out disc herniation
The test was performed on the wrong leg
items.explanation: The crossed SLR is the mirror image of the SLR: poor sensitivity, high specificity (88%). Reproducing the symptomatic leg's pain by raising the OTHER leg suggests a large or medial herniation tensioning the root from across the midline. Positive = informative; negative = meaningless.
items.pearl: SLR to rule out, crossed SLR to rule in. Learn them as a pair.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: 34-year-old warehouse worker. Sharp low back pain lifting yesterday, now shooting pain down the right leg to the lateral foot, worse with sitting and coughing. Rank the differentials.
orderedOptions: Non-specific low back pain with somatic referral
items.explanation: Below-knee dermatomal pain + worse with sitting/valsalva (cough) after a flexion-load injury is the disc-radiculopathy signature. Somatic referral is the main alternative but rarely projects to the foot. Facet pain is typically extension-loaded and stays proximal. Stenosis is a condition of older spines and standing/walking aggravation — the opposite pattern.

items.stem: 72-year-old with bilateral leg heaviness and calf pain after walking 200 m, relieved within minutes of sitting down. Can cycle for an hour without symptoms. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: Walking-induced bilateral leg symptoms relieved by SITTING (spinal flexion) — and crucially, unlimited CYCLING tolerance (flexed posture) — is neurogenic claudication. Vascular claudication is the must-exclude twin: it stops with standing still (no posture change needed) and would limit cycling too. That one history detail — the bike — does the discriminating.
items.pearl: Ask claudicants about cycling. The bike separates the spine from the arteries.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: 26-year-old man, 8 months of low back and buttock pain. Worst in the second half of the night and early morning, stiffness >1 hour, clearly better with exercise, worse with rest. Rank the differentials.
items.explanation: Age <45, insidious onset >3 months, night-dominant pain, prolonged morning stiffness, better with exercise, worse with rest — the inflammatory back pain pattern. Diagnostic delay for axial SpA averages 7+ YEARS, largely because it sits unrecognized in MSK caseloads labelled 'mechanical LBP'. Mechanical pain behaves the opposite way with rest and activity.

items.stem: 41-year-old, 2 weeks of low back pain and right leg pain, worse since yesterday. Select every finding that forms part of the cauda equina syndrome picture requiring EMERGENCY referral.

findings.text: Numbness when wiping after using the toilet
findings.note: Saddle anaesthesia — often first noticed exactly this way. Ask directly; patients rarely volunteer it.

findings.text: Difficulty starting urination and reduced sensation of bladder fullness
findings.note: Urinary retention with reduced sensation is the most consistent CES feature. Painless retention with overflow is a late, grave sign.

findings.text: New pain now shooting down BOTH legs
findings.note: Progression to bilateral radicular pain suggests central canal compromise — a key escalation signal.

findings.text: New erectile dysfunction since symptoms worsened
findings.note: Sexual dysfunction is a core CES symptom and the least-asked-about. It belongs in every CES screen.

findings.text: Pain worse with coughing and sneezing
findings.note: Valsalva aggravation is standard discogenic behaviour — common in uncomplicated radiculopathy.

findings.text: Right foot pins and needles in a single dermatome
findings.note: Unilateral single-dermatome paraesthesia is routine radiculopathy, not CES — it's the SPREAD beyond one root that alarms.

items.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome: saddle anaesthesia, bladder dysfunction, bilateral leg symptoms, sexual dysfunction. Suspicion = same-day emergency MRI — the window for surgical decompression before permanent bladder/bowel damage is measured in hours. Every LBP patient with leg symptoms gets the verbal CES screen, and every clinician needs the words to ask it without embarrassment.
items.pearl: You cannot screen for CES without saying the words 'bladder', 'bowels', and 'sexual function' out loud.

items.stem: 63-year-old with 7 weeks of thoracolumbar pain. Select the genuine malignancy red flags.

findings.text: History of prostate cancer 4 years ago
findings.note: Prostate is one of the classic bone-metastasizing primaries (with breast, lung, kidney, thyroid). Past cancer + new spinal pain = investigate.

findings.text: Pain is constant, gnawing, and no position gives relief
findings.note: Non-mechanical, position-independent pain is the malignancy pattern — mechanical pain has better and worse positions.

findings.text: Waking in the early hours with pain despite medication
findings.note: In combination with the rest of this picture, unremitting night pain supports escalation — alone it is weak, together it is loud.

findings.text: Pain aggravated by prolonged sitting
findings.note: Postural aggravation is mechanical behaviour.

findings.text: Age 63
findings.note: Age >50 raises baseline risk and lowers your threshold, but age alone is a modifier, not a flag to act on by itself.

findings.text: Stiffness easing 20 minutes after getting up
findings.note: Brief morning stiffness that eases is benign and common.

items.explanation: No single feature diagnoses spinal malignancy — history of cancer is the strongest single item (raising probability substantially), and the combination of cancer history + non-mechanical constant pain + night dominance demands investigation. Red flags work as clusters and trajectories, not as a checklist of isolated items.

items.stem: 76-year-old woman with sudden severe mid-lumbar pain after lifting a flowerpot. Select the features pointing to vertebral fragility fracture.

findings.text: Long-term oral corticosteroids for polymyalgia rheumatica
findings.note: Steroids + age = high osteoporosis risk. Steroid use is one of the strongest fracture red flags.

findings.text: Sudden onset with a trivial load in an osteoporosis-risk patient
findings.note: In fragile bone, a flowerpot IS major trauma. Sudden severe pain with trivial loading fits acute vertebral collapse.

findings.text: Pain is sharply worse with any transitional movement, eases lying still
findings.note: Severe movement-triggered pain easing with stillness fits acute fracture mechanics — and helps distinguish it from malignancy's constant pain.

findings.text: She recalls being 3 cm taller in her forties
findings.note: Height loss suggests previous silent vertebral fractures — most vertebral fractures are never diagnosed.

findings.text: No leg pain or neurological symptoms
findings.note: Reassuring, and typical — most osteoporotic fractures don't compromise neural tissue. Its absence isn't a flag; it just doesn't exclude fracture.

items.explanation: Thoracolumbar pain + trivial trauma + steroid/osteoporosis risk = X-ray before manual therapy or exercise loading. Note the discriminating texture: fracture pain is typically severe but MECHANICAL (movement-triggered, eased by stillness), unlike malignancy's constant gnaw.

items.stem: 48-year-old with 3 weeks of worsening thoracolumbar pain. Select the features suggesting spinal infection (discitis/vertebral osteomyelitis).

findings.text: Fevers and drenching night sweats
findings.note: Systemic infective features with spinal pain = infection until excluded. Note: fever is absent in up to half of confirmed cases, so its absence never excludes.

findings.text: IV drug use
findings.note: A major risk factor for haematogenous spread to the spine — with immunosuppression, diabetes, and recent bacteraemia.

findings.text: Recent urinary tract infection treated 5 weeks ago
findings.note: A recent infective source is exactly how organisms seed the spine. Always ask about recent infections, procedures, and dental work.

findings.text: Pain is unrelenting and progressing week on week despite rest and analgesia
findings.note: Relentless progression is the trajectory red flag — benign LBP fluctuates and trends better.

findings.text: Pain began after helping a friend move house
findings.note: A plausible mechanical trigger — but a trigger explains onset, not a progressive worsening course with systemic features.

items.explanation: Spinal infection is rare but devastating when missed — average diagnostic delay is 2–4 months because it masquerades as mechanical pain. The pattern: progressive unrelenting pain + infective risk factor + (sometimes) systemic signs. Bloods (ESR/CRP) and MRI, urgently.

items.stem: Both cause leg pain on walking in older adults. Which question best discriminates?
options: What do you have to DO for the pain to ease — stop and stand, or sit down/lean forward?
How far can you walk before the pain starts?
Is the pain in one leg or both?
Does the pain throb?
items.explanation: Vascular claudication is a supply-demand problem: stopping is enough, in any position. Neurogenic claudication is a canal-space problem: relief needs spinal FLEXION — sitting, leaning on the trolley, crouching. Walking distance, laterality, and pain quality all overlap. Follow up with the bicycle question and pedal pulses.
items.pearl: The supermarket-trolley lean is a physical exam finding the patient performs for you.
items.citation: UNVERIFIED — prototype draft; citation pending clinical review

items.stem: A patient has back and leg pain. Which feature best identifies the leg pain as radicular rather than somatic referral?
options: Sharp, narrow-band pain below the knee with paraesthesia in a dermatomal distribution
Aching in the buttock and posterior thigh
Leg pain that worsens when the back pain worsens
Tenderness over the piriformis
items.explanation: Radicular pain travels in a narrow band, typically below the knee, often lancinating, with paraesthesia/numbness in the root's territory — and neuro signs when conduction is affected. Somatic referral is deep, achy, poorly localized, and stays proximal (buttock/thigh). The distinction matters: management, prognosis conversations, and escalation criteria differ.

items.stem: Which single history feature best discriminates inflammatory from mechanical back pain?
options: Whether pain improves with exercise but NOT with rest
Pain severity
Presence of buttock pain
Age under 45
items.explanation: The response-to-activity pattern is the sharpest single discriminator: inflammatory pain improves with movement and worsens with rest (hence night/morning dominance); mechanical pain generally likes rest and dislikes provocation. Age <45 is a prerequisite rather than a discriminator, and severity/buttock pain discriminate nothing. Screen further with morning-stiffness duration, alternating buttock pain, psoriasis/uveitis/IBD history.

items.stem: 65-year-old with 'low back and thigh pain'. Which finding best points to the HIP as the source?
options: Groin pain with restricted, painful passive hip internal rotation
Pain radiating below the knee
Pain on lumbar extension
Tenderness over the greater trochanter
items.explanation: Groin pain + loss of internal rotation is the classic hip OA signature — IR is typically the first and most affected motion. Below-knee radiation points spinal; lumbar extension pain points spinal; trochanteric tenderness suggests lateral hip (gluteal tendinopathy), a third diagnosis entirely. Hip-spine syndrome is common: examine both in every 'back and leg' presentation over 60.
items.pearl: No LBP exam in an older adult is complete without passive hip internal rotation.
